scams.name: Madrid Barajas (MAD) Airport Taxi Overcharge
scams.description: You land at Madrid Barajas after a long flight and take the taxi queue outside Terminal 4. The legal Madrid airport flat fare to anywhere inside the M-30 ring road (including the city center, Retiro, Salamanca, Chueca neighborhoods) is €33. Drivers who claim the meter is broken or add 'luggage fees,' 'terminal transfer fees,' or 'night surcharges' are running one of Europe's most-documented airport scams. Community reports document specific cases where drivers charged €60–€110 for €33 rides. The 'legal' variant is especially insidious — drivers obey the meter but take an indirect route via the M-40 ring road instead of the M-11/M-30, adding 20 minutes and €20 to the fare. One traveler wrote: the driver added a flat 'airport fee' charge before the meter even started. Terminal-to-terminal taxis at Barajas run a separate shakedown — quoting €30–€50 for what should be €5 or a free shuttle bus. Your protection: the Madrid airport flat rate to anywhere inside the M-30 is €33 — posted on signs at every Barajas taxi queue. Anything quoted above that is overcharging. For terminal transfers, take the free Airport Shuttle bus (yellow, 'Bus Express 12') rather than a taxi. Alternatives to taxi: Metro Line 8 runs directly from all Barajas terminals to Nuevos Ministerios for €5 (includes the €3 Barajas supplement; 30 minutes); the Renfe Cercanías C-1 commuter train from Terminal 4 to Atocha or Chamartín is €2.60 (25 minutes). Use Uber, Bolt, FreeNow, or Cabify for app-regulated fares; all four work in Madrid with digital receipts.
scams.avoidance: Demand the €33 flat rate for anywhere inside the M-30 — posted on signs at the queue Take Metro Line 8 from Barajas to Nuevos Ministerios (€5, 30 min, scam-free) Or Renfe Cercanías C-1 from T4 to Atocha or Chamartín (€2.60, 25 min) Between terminals, use the free Bus Express 12 yellow shuttle — not a taxi For app taxis, use Uber, Bolt, FreeNow, or Cabify — all show fixed prices
scams.location: Madrid Barajas Airport (MAD) Terminal 1, T4 taxi rank, cruise-connection transfers

scams.name: Metro Sol + Atocha Pickpocket Teams
scams.description: Madrid Metro is otherwise clean and safe, but two corridors see concentrated pickpocket activity: Line 1 (Atocha–Sol–Chamartín, the airport-to-center axis) and the Sol station transfer concourse where Lines 1, 2, and 3 meet. Teams operate in three- or four-person groups — one distracts, one lifts, one receives, one keeps lookout. Community reports document tourists hit at Atocha while transferring trains, and the airport-Metro run: 'I had no issues with pickpockets but I was attacked while walking to the Atocha train station to head to Barcelona.' The most common 2025 patterns: fake crowd crush at carriage doors where someone pushes from behind while another reaches into your outer pocket; 'map distraction' where someone asks for directions with a large open map blocking your view of your bag; escalator bump where a passenger 'falls' into you. Travelers offer the comparative context: 'Madrid is much safer than Barcelona. Do not put your valuables in a backpack on your back. Keep your wallet/passport front pocket.' The same threads note pickpocket teams rotate between Barcelona and Madrid's Gran Vía/Sol stretch seasonally. The damage is typically a phone (€600–€1,200 replacement for a current iPhone) or a wallet (€50–€300 cash plus card cancellation overhead). For insurance, you need a Policía Nacional report filed at a police station within 24 hours — Comisaría de Centro at Calle Leganitos 19 handles tourist reports. Your protection: wear a zipped crossbody bag in front of you in any crowded environment; never use a backpack's outer pocket; keep phone in a zipped inner pocket, not a back pocket; do not pull out your phone on crowded escalators or at carriage doors. At Atocha train station specifically, keep bags between your knees when seated waiting for trains.
scams.avoidance: Wear a zipped anti-theft crossbody bag in front of you in any crowded environment Keep phone in a zipped inner pocket or jacket pocket; never in a back pocket Split cash across pockets — €20 front pocket, rest in a money belt or hotel safe Do not pull out phone on crowded escalators, at carriage doors, or on Line 1 at rush hour Report thefts at Comisaría de Centro (Calle Leganitos 19) within 24 hours for insurance
scams.location: Metro Line 1 (Atocha-Sol-Chamartín), Sol station transfers, Gran Vía and Callao stations

scams.name: Bird Poop Distraction Pickpocket
scams.description: You are walking across Puerta del Sol when you feel something wet hit your shoulder — 'bird poop,' but suspiciously mustard-yellow or cream-colored. A friendly bystander appears immediately with tissues and helps you wipe it off while expressing sympathy. You thank them and walk on; ten minutes later you realize your wallet is gone. One traveler wrote: 'That happened to me in Madrid years ago. Mustard on my jacket.' Community reports describe the mechanic precisely: 'They pick pocket you while they help wipe off the fake bird poop.' The scam teams operate at Puerta del Sol (the Kilometre Zero plaza in central Madrid), Plaza Mayor, along Gran Vía, and near tourist photo spots like the Bear and Strawberry Tree statue. The pattern is flagged across Barcelona, Madrid, and Lisbon. The 'poop' is typically mustard, ketchup, shaving cream, or paint — sprayed from a pocket-sized bottle as you pass. The 'helpful stranger' appears within seconds, carrying tissues already in hand — the giveaway that they were expecting this 'accident.' Your protection: if you feel something wet hit you unexpectedly, do NOT stop to examine or clean it. Walk immediately to a nearby café, shop, or hotel lobby — a secure indoor space — before dealing with the stain. Do not accept help from any stranger who appears immediately. The stain will wash out later; your wallet and phone are the priority. Keep valuables in a zipped front pocket or crossbody bag worn in front. If you were pickpocketed, file at Comisaría de Centro (Calle Leganitos 19) within 24 hours for insurance documentation. Madrid Policía Nacional takes these reports seriously — Spain's Ministry of Interior has published warnings about the bird-poop variant specifically.
scams.avoidance: If hit by something wet unexpectedly, walk IMMEDIATELY to an indoor space (café, shop, hotel) Do not accept help from any stranger who appears within seconds of the 'accident' Keep valuables in a zipped front pocket or crossbody bag worn in front Photograph the 'helpers' from a distance if you have time — useful for police report File at Comisaría de Centro within 24 hours if pickpocketed for insurance claim
scams.location: Puerta del Sol, Plaza Mayor, Gran Vía walking routes, tourist photo spots

scams.name: Puerta del Sol Bracelet & Clipboard Petition Scam
scams.description: A young woman approaches at Puerta del Sol with a clipboard — 'signing a petition for deaf children.' You stop to listen. She gestures for you to sign. While you hold the pen, a partner opens your day-bag from behind, and a third accomplice tries to tie a colorful 'friendship bracelet' to your wrist. One traveler wrote: 'Tourist from the US here. Got approached by 2 girls with clipboards asking for some petition for disabled children.' The team operates at Puerta del Sol, Plaza Mayor, the entrance to the Royal Palace (Palacio Real), and the Temple of Debod — all high tourist-foot-traffic zones. The bracelet component is the same Syntagma/Athens mechanic. Another traveler witnessed it: 'I did witness the bracelet scam where a guy hands someone a bracelet and then won't take it back.' The charity petition adds a social-obligation hook specifically targeting older travelers — the 'deaf children' or 'disabled orphans' framing is designed to make you feel guilty about walking away. No legitimate Spanish charity collects signatures from tourists in Puerta del Sol; the Spanish Federation of Deaf People and ONCE (the National Organisation of the Spanish Blind) use verifiable volunteer kiosks with uniforms, not clipboard teams. Your protection: if anyone approaches with a clipboard or bracelet, cross your arms and step back immediately. Do not stop to read the clipboard, do not make eye contact, and do not slow your walking pace. Say 'no, gracias' firmly and keep moving. If a bracelet is already on your wrist, walk to a café and cut it off with scissors — do not pay anything. Keep your wallet in a front zipped pocket and your phone in an inner jacket pocket when walking through Puerta del Sol, Plaza Mayor, or near the Royal Palace. These scams peak in April–October; Policía Nacional's Unit for Tourism Assistance (SATE) patrols Puerta del Sol during summer evenings.
scams.avoidance: Cross your arms and step back if approached with a clipboard or bracelet Say 'no, gracias' firmly and keep walking — do not engage Legitimate Spanish charities (ONCE, Federación de Personas Sordas) use uniformed kiosks, not clipboard teams Keep wallet in front zipped pocket or crossbody bag worn in front at Puerta del Sol Report persistent crews to SATE (Tourism Assistance police) — active summer patrols at Puerta del Sol
scams.location: Puerta del Sol, Plaza Mayor, Royal Palace (Palacio Real), Temple of Debod

scams.name: Fake Prado Museum & Royal Palace 'Skip-the-Line' Ticket Websites
scams.description: You plan ahead. Weeks before your trip you search 'Prado Museum tickets' and click the first result — a professional-looking site named something like myprado-tickets.com or prado-skiptheline.es. You pay €35 per person for 'skip-the-line' tickets. At the Prado entrance on arrival, the QR codes scan as invalid. One traveler wrote: 'I've tried to buy tickets from Prado's official website but it's glitchy. It keeps asking for a confirmation email address even though I had entered one' — fraud sites exploit the real site's technical issues to funnel tourists. The only official Prado ticket website is museodelprado.es. The Royal Palace (Palacio Real) official tickets are at patrimonionacional.es. Tickets outside these two domains from any 'skip-the-line' or 'official Spain ticket' reseller should be treated with suspicion. Legitimate third-party resellers with customs guarantees include GetYourGuide, Viator, and Tiqets. Community reports reference Prado and Royal Palace tour quality — tours with licensed Spanish guides are legitimate; 'official skip-the-line' tickets at 2x the posted price are resale scams. The Prado posted admission is €15 (or free for the final two hours daily, 6–8 PM, currently as of 2025). The Royal Palace admission is €14. If a reseller charges €35 per person for 'skip-the-line' access that should cost €15–€14, they are marking up the ticket 100–130% — and in the worst case producing fake QR codes entirely. At the site, buy tickets at the official booth or use the free-entry window if budget is the issue. Licensed Spanish tour guides wear a Ministry of Tourism-issued credential (a yellow card with Ministerio de Industria seal); ask to see it before hiring a guide on-site. Pay by credit card for any online ticket purchase; chargeback window is 60–120 days in most jurisdictions.
scams.avoidance: Book Prado tickets only at museodelprado.es; Royal Palace only at patrimonionacional.es Verified third-party resellers: GetYourGuide, Viator, Tiqets (credit card with chargeback) Search the domain name plus 'scam' before paying any online Madrid ticket seller At the Prado, visit in the free 6–8 PM window if budget is the issue Licensed Spanish tour guides wear a Ministerio de Industria yellow credential card — ask to see it
scams.location: Online booking before arrival; touts selling printed vouchers outside Prado and Palacio Real

scams.name: Puerta del Sol & Plaza Mayor Tourist-Menu Restaurant Overcharge
scams.description: You sit at a Plaza Mayor arcade restaurant for lunch. You order paella, a Spanish salad, and two glasses of wine. Bread and olives arrive — unrequested. The bill totals €85. The menu outside showed paella at €18; at the table it was €32. 'Welcome' bread, olives, and a small plate of Manchego added €12. Community reports consistently flag Plaza Mayor arcade restaurants as overpriced tourist traps. One traveler captured the community view: 'It's difficult to go wrong with food. In any case, avoid places very close to tourist attractions and the classic tourist traps.' The mechanic is opaque pricing plus 'optional' extras that arrive unordered. Restaurants on Puerta del Sol's perimeter, around Plaza Mayor's arcades, and along Gran Vía's tourist spine often serve bread, olives, and small tapas 'as a welcome' — each appearing on the bill at €3–€10. The menu at the entrance may show lower prices than the one at the table, or the 'tourist menu del día' may have fine print adding 'bebidas' (drinks) and 'postre' (dessert) at premium prices. Spanish consumer law (Ley General para la Defensa de los Consumidores) requires prices to be clearly disclosed; restaurants violating this can be fined, but enforcement on Plaza Mayor is weak. Your protection: read the menu at the entrance before sitting, and confirm prices at the table match when the menu arrives. Decline any 'welcome' items explicitly when they arrive — 'no, gracias' is enough. Count the bill line by line against the menu you ordered from. For genuine Spanish food at local prices, walk one block away from the main tourist spine: La Latina, Chueca, and Malasaña all have well-reviewed, honestly-priced tapas bars (Casa Lucio, Casa Labra, Bodega de la Ardosa are community-respected for transparent pricing). The 'menu del día' tradition is a Spanish lunch institution — €12–€18 for starter, main, bread, drink, and dessert — but only at restaurants outside the tourist triangle. On Plaza Mayor the same 'menu del día' is often €25–€30 with worse food.
scams.avoidance: Read the menu at the entrance before sitting; confirm prices at the table match Decline 'welcome' items explicitly — 'no, gracias' politely waves them off Eat one block away from Plaza Mayor — La Latina, Chueca, Malasaña have fair-priced local tapas bars Community-respected posted-price Madrid options: Casa Lucio, Casa Labra, Bodega de la Ardosa Proper 'menu del día' is €12–€18 at local restaurants — anything above €22 on Plaza Mayor is tourist pricing
scams.location: Puerta del Sol perimeter, Plaza Mayor arcade restaurants, Gran Vía tourist spine

scams.name: Hotel & Booking Off-Platform Payment Fraud
scams.description: Three days before your Madrid arrival, an email appears in your inbox that looks exactly like Booking.com — same logo, same color scheme, same footer. The message says your payment needs to be finalised through a 'secure link.' The URL is close but not identical: booking-com.net, bookingcom-pay.org, or similar. You pay €450; on arrival, the real hotel has no record of the payment, and your original Booking.com reservation appears to have been cancelled. Community reports document that the Booking.com impersonation scam hits Madrid hotels as frequently as Athens or Barcelona, and confirm the mechanic: scammers infiltrate the Booking.com chat system itself, impersonating hotel staff. A Madrid-specific variant targets the Airbnb and short-term rental market in Chueca, Malasaña, and Lavapiés — neighborhoods with high tourist demand and dense apartment conversion. Operators create lookalike listings using photos stolen from legitimate properties, accept deposits, and cancel 48 hours before arrival citing 'water damage' with an offer to relocate you to an 'alternative' that requires off-platform cash payment. Community reports flag booking verification as a genuine concern. In 2025, Ekathimerini-style Spanish media has reported organized Airbnb fraud rings operating in Madrid, with Policía Nacional making arrests during a May 2025 operation. Your protection: book only through Booking.com, Hotels.com, Expedia, or Airbnb with credit card payment and screenshot all confirmations. Never click payment links in emails, even ones that appear to come from the booking platform — log into the platform directly through a fresh browser tab and check your reservation status. Call the hotel through the Google Maps phone number (not the one in any recent email) to verify any payment request. Read the most recent 30 days of hotel reviews looking for 'payment link,' 'water damage,' or 'moved to sister property' complaints. Pay only by credit card for chargeback protection (60–120 days). For Madrid peak season (April–October and Christmas markets), book six or more weeks ahead through official channels to reduce exposure to last-minute 'deal' messages.
scams.avoidance: Book only through Booking.com, Hotels.com, Expedia, Airbnb with credit card — screenshot confirmations Never click payment links in emails; log into booking account directly in a fresh browser tab Call the hotel through the Google Maps number (not the email's) to verify any request Pay only by credit card — chargeback is your strongest protection (60–120 days) Book six or more weeks ahead for peak season (April–October, Christmas)
scams.location: Citywide Madrid — advertised as Sol, Gran Vía, Chueca, Salamanca district hotels
